archetype.name: Gunslinger (deep-ball)
archetype.definition: A pocket thrower whose downfield accuracy produces most of his value and whose willingness to fit tight windows has always come with a heavy interception bill.

report.headline: Deep ball is real; protection, screens and interceptions are draining it
report.take:
Darnold arrived at this season off two strong years. In 2025 he posted 0.162 EPA per play, ranked 14th, with 8.49 yards per attempt, ranked 5th, and a 5.2 CPOE. The 2026 version reads very differently: -0.051 EPA per dropback, 30th of 45, and an 8-interception, 4.5% pick rate that ranks 41st. The dossier's start credit is muddled. It lists Drew Lock as the Week 2-6 starter, yet the game log has Darnold on 100% of snaps Weeks 3-6. What matters is the 177 attempts in the game log, and that he is QB1 again with Lock out with an elbow injury.

The split by depth explains most of the season. Throws of 10+ air yards are worth +23.7 EPA, and the 17 deep attempts carry 1.055 EPA apiece with a 17.9 CPOE. Everything under 10 yards adds up to -13.1, and nearly all of that comes from the 37 throws behind the line, worth -14.1 in total. Those screens and dump-offs are eating a struggling offense alive. Third down (-12.6) and one-score game states (-25.1) are where the damage lands. Both point to obvious passing downs behind a line that allows hits at the 30th-ranked rate. He is pressured on 30.4% of dropbacks, 37th of 38.

The numbers also hide that his accuracy is fine. His bad-throw rate of 9.6% ranks 3rd and is better than last year's 13.6%. His aggressiveness is up 6.2 points and his time to throw is up to 3.01 seconds. The interceptions come from holding the ball and forcing windows under pressure, not from scattershot ball placement. That has been in his career every year: his interception counts ranked 48th or worse in every full season.

The Week 7 KC game is the template. He got the ball out in 2.45 seconds, took zero sacks and posted +12.2 EPA against the 5th-ranked defense. If the staff keeps that quicker rhythm and keeps feeding Jaxon Smith-Njigba (+33.8 EPA on 57 targets), the efficiency should drift back toward average. The interception rate should fall, but not to league average.

strengths.title: Downfield accuracy carries the offense
strengths.body: His 17 deep attempts produce 1.055 EPA each with a 17.9 CPOE, and the 10+ air-yard group adds up to +23.7. Seventeen throws is a small sample and the CPOE will cool. Still, he ranked top-10 in CPOE in both 2024 and 2025, so the skill is real even if this level isn't.

strengths.title: Clean ball placement despite turnovers
strengths.body: A 9.6% bad-throw rate ranks 3rd of 38 and improved on last season. That separates his interceptions from inaccuracy. They come from decisions and pressure, which are more fixable with a quicker game plan than a mechanical problem would be.

strengths.title: A true No. 1 target
strengths.body: Smith-Njigba has drawn 57 targets at 0.593 EPA apiece, by far the biggest positive in the passing game. That concentration is sustainable as long as Darnold keeps looking his way. It also explains why the offense's pass EPA ranks a respectable 18th despite Darnold's individual struggles.

concerns.title: Interceptions are his lasting flaw
concerns.body: A 4.5% interception rate ranks 41st, and his career shows this is identity rather than a blip: 14 interceptions ranked 61st of 63 last year. Aggressiveness is up 6.2 points this season, which pushes the rate higher. Expect fewer than his current pace of 23, but still more than most starters.

concerns.title: Protection is collapsing, and Cross is doubtful
concerns.body: He is pressured on 30.4% of dropbacks and the offense ranks 30th in hit rate allowed. Most of the damage shows up on third down. Left tackle Charles Cross, a 98%-snap starter, is doubtful with a high ankle sprain, which makes holding the ball for three seconds even riskier.

concerns.title: Behind-the-line throws are wasted plays
concerns.body: Screens and dump-offs have a 21.6% success rate and a -14.1 EPA total, which cancels most of what the deep game earns. That is partly scheme and partly a broken run game: the offense's rush EPA ranks 29th and Charbonnet is out with a torn ACL. It's fixable through play-calling more than through Darnold himself.

trend.note: He swung from +4.1 EPA in the 379-yard Washington shootout to -12 against San Francisco and -6.7 on 51 attempts in Denver. Then he got the ball out quickly against KC for +12.2. The last three games (-0.056 per dropback) are essentially his season rate, with fewer touchdowns.

nextGame.headline: Chicago's leaky deep coverage meets his best skill, if he's protected
nextGame.body:
Chicago is the worst deep-pass defense in the dossier: 1.345 EPA allowed on deep throws, rank 32, and 30th in explosive pass rate. That lines up directly with Darnold's strength. The catch is that the Bears are stingy underneath (short EPA rank 5) and get home, with a sack rate that ranks 3rd. The game rewards exactly the hold-and-launch approach that has produced his worst plays this season. Chicago's offense ranks 11th in EPA and the total is 46.5, so this could turn into a game where he has to keep throwing.

Availability cuts both ways. Seattle likely loses Cross at left tackle, which is the biggest risk to the deep shots. Rashid Shaheed is questionable, though his -0.452 EPA per target makes his absence less costly than it sounds. Chicago is without LB T.J. Edwards (88% of snaps), and CB Malik Muhammad II (75%) is questionable with a toe injury. That thins the coverage Darnold will attack over the middle and outside.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus the league's worst deep defense
keyMatchups.body: Darnold's deep throws are worth 1.055 EPA each, and Chicago gives up 1.345 per deep pass. If he gets time, this is where the game's efficiency lives. Smith-Njigba is the obvious beneficiary.

keyMatchups.title: Bears' rush against a backup tackle
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's sack rate ranks 3rd, and Seattle's line already allows hits at a bottom-three rate. Without Cross, the quick game he used against KC (2.45-second time to throw, zero sacks) is the counter. Whether the staff leans on it matters more than any coverage matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end opening for Barner
keyMatchups.body: Chicago allows 0.44 EPA per target to the top tight end, 27th, and Edwards' absence weakens the second level. AJ Barner has been a negative so far at -0.35 EPA per target. This is the spot for him to turn that around.

nextGame.watch: His time to throw: if it stays near the KC game's 2.45 seconds with a backup at left tackle, he can exploit Chicago's deep coverage; if it drifts back past three seconds, the sacks and interceptions return.

restOfSeason.body:
The deep efficiency will cool from 17.9 CPOE, but the skill is backed by top-10 CPOE in each of the last two seasons and a 3rd-ranked bad-throw rate. The things most likely to improve are the interception and touchdown rates. A 1.9% TD rate over the last three games is too low for an offense with Smith-Njigba, and an interception rate near 4.5% sits even above his own turnover-prone norm. Expect something like 225-265 passing yards a game with 1.2-1.8 touchdowns and roughly one interception a game. That points to roughly average efficiency rather than last year's top-15 level.

The ceiling depends on protection and play design more than on him. With Cross out and the run game 29th in EPA, defenses can tee off on obvious passing downs. Seattle's 2nd-ranked defense keeps game scripts close, which means more of the one-score dropbacks where he has been worst. Lock's elbow is also a variable. He is listed with a return estimate, so Darnold has to play well to keep a firm hold on the job.
swingFactors: Charles Cross's ankle and pass protection
How much the staff uses the quick game
Drew Lock's elbow and the QB job

confidence.note: Six games and 17 deep attempts, conflicting start records, and an unsettled QB room and line.
